scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Rhumba originated in the 1930s on the US East Coast, blending Afro-Cuban son cubano rhythms with American big band music.
The 1930 recording of 'El manisero' by Don Azpiazú's Havana Casino Orchestra in New York was pivotal, becoming the first Latin song to sell 1 million copies in the US.
This sparked the rhumba craze, followed by Cuban artists like Armando Oréfiche and the Lecuona Cuban Boys touring internationally.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Rhumba is danced socially and in international ballroom competitions worldwide.
It is appreciated for its sensuality and musicality, reflecting Afro-Cuban roots in its hip movements and partner interaction.
The dance is not sacred or restricted.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Rhumba music combines Afro-Cuban rhythms such as son cubano, conga, and rumba with American big band instrumentation.
The 1930 hit 'El manisero' featured saxophones, cornets, banjo, guitar, piano, violin, bass, and trap drums, with vocals and a trumpet solo.
Listen for the saxophones, cornets, banjo, guitar.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 96 beats a minute.
A blend of Afro-Cuban son rhythms with American big band swing, featuring melodic trumpet solos, smooth vocals, and a steady 4/4 beat that supports sensual hip movements.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Don Azpiazú, whose 1930 recording 'El manisero' launched the rhumba craze; Monsieur Pierre (Pierre Zurcher-Margolle), who codified the International style after studying Cuban dancers in 1947, 1951, and 1953; bandleaders Xavier Cugat, Jimmy Dorsey, Nathaniel Shilkret, Leo Reisman, and Enric Madriguera.
Two main ballroom styles: American style with slow-quick-quick box step and International style with quick-quick-slow pattern.
Rhumba derives from Afro-Cuban son cubano, conga, and rumba rhythms, adapted by American big bands in the 1930s.

visual_brief.setting_notes: Rhumba is danced socially and in international ballroom competitions worldwide. It is appreciated for its sensuality and musicality, reflecting Afro-Cuban roots in its hip movements and partner interaction. The dance is not sacred or restricted. It symbolizes flirtation and attraction between partners, with the man typically responding to the woman's movements.

steps_as_taught.name: Basic Step
steps_as_taught.description: Consists of a step to the side, a forward break, and a back break.

steps_as_taught.name: New York
steps_as_taught.description: Consists of a side step and a forward break, connected by a 90-degree change of direction.

steps_as_taught.name: Spot Turn
steps_as_taught.description: A turn that can be danced solo or used by the follower to dance an underarm turn.

steps_as_taught.name: Hand to Hand
steps_as_taught.description: The opposite of a New York, where you cross over into a back break on count 2.

steps_as_taught.name: Basic in Place
steps_as_taught.description: Simply stepping together to the Rumba rhythm.

steps_as_taught.name: Open Basic
steps_as_taught.description: Contains a forward step and a back step, connected by a forward break and a back break.

steps_as_taught.name: Alternative Basic
steps_as_taught.description: Similar to the basic step, but you step together on counts 2 and 3.

steps_as_taught.name: Progressive Walks Forward & Back
steps_as_taught.description: Can be linked and danced continuously.

steps_as_taught.name: Side Basic Step
steps_as_taught.description: Step side and change weight from foot to foot

steps_as_taught.name: Basic
steps_as_taught.description: Rock forward, replace, side, rock back, replace, side
